title: Current Electricity & RC Circuits
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Microscopic Drift Velocity, Ohm's Law, Resistivity & Temperature Dependence, Kirchhoff's Laws, Nodal & Symmetry Networks, Cells & Maximum Power Theorem, Wheatstone/Meter Bridge, Potentiometer, Ammeter/Voltmeter & RC Transients
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: From Static Charges to Steady Electric Current

In Chapters 15 and 16, we studied Electrostatics—where free electrons inside a metal conductor quickly rearrange themselves until the internal electric field becomes zero ($\vec{E}_{\text{inside}} = 0$) and all motion stops.

What if we connect the two ends of a metal wire across a battery that maintains a constant potential difference $V$? Now the internal electric field $E = V/L$ never disappears! Free electrons are continuously pushed by the field, colliding with positive metal ions and drifting steadily at a slow average speed ($v_d \sim 10^{-4}\text{ m/s}$). This continuous, directed flow of charge is called Electric Current ($I$).

Why Does Electric Current Have an Arrow Direction Yet Behave as a Scalar?
Even though we draw an arrow on circuit wires to show the direction of conventional current (the direction in which positive charge flows, opposite to electron drift), Electric Current $I$ is a SCALAR quantity! Why? Because currents meeting at a wire junction add by simple algebraic addition ($I_1 + I_2 = I_3$), completely independent of the geometric angle between the wires! (However, Current Density $\vec{J} = \frac{I}{A}\hat{n}$ IS a true vector!).

topics.title: Electric Current, Drift Velocity, Mobility, Microscopic Ohm's Law, Wire Stretching & Temperature Dependence of Resistance
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Instantaneous Current, Average Current & Current Density Vector ($\vec{J}$)
$$\text{Instantaneous Current:} \; \boxed{I(t) = \frac{dq}{dt} \iff \Delta q = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} I(t)\,dt} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Average Current:} \; \boxed{I_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta q}{\Delta t}} \qquad (1\text{ A} = 1\text{ C/s})$$

If a point charge $q$ revolves in a circle of radius $r$ at speed $v$ (or frequency $f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}$), the equivalent current is $\boxed{I = \frac{q}{T} = q f = \frac{q v}{2\pi r} = \frac{q\omega}{2\pi}}$.

$$\text{Current Density Vector } (\vec{J}, \text{ Unit: } \text{A/m}^2): \qquad \boxed{I = \int \vec{J}\cdot d\vec{A} = J A \cos\theta}$$
1.2 Microscopic Drift Velocity ($v_d$), Mobility ($\mu$) & Ohm's Law
Thermal Speed vs. Drift Speed vs. Signal Speed inside a Copper Wire:
• Random Thermal Speed ($v_{\text{rms}} \sim 10^5\text{ m/s}$): High-speed zig-zag motion due to room temperature; net average velocity is zero.
• Drift Speed ($v_d \sim 10^{-4}\text{ m/s} = 0.1\text{ mm/s}$): Tiny net average velocity acquired by free electrons opposite to $\vec{E}$ between collisions (relaxation time $\tau \sim 10^{-14}\text{ s}$).
• Electric Field Signal Speed ($\sim c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$): Why the bulb lights up the instant you flip the switch!
$$\text{1. Drift Velocity:} \quad \boxed{\vec{v}_d = -\left(\frac{e\tau}{m}\right)\vec{E}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{2. Mobility:} \quad \boxed{\mu = \frac{|v_d|}{E} = \frac{e\tau}{m}} \quad (\text{Unit: } \text{m}^2\text{V}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1})$$
$$\text{3. Current vs. Drift Speed:} \qquad \boxed{I = n e A v_d \iff J = n e v_d} \qquad (n = \text{free electrons per unit volume } \text{m}^{-3})$$
$$\text{4. Ohm's Law (Vector & Macroscopic):} \quad \boxed{\vec{J} = \sigma \vec{E} = \frac{1}{\rho}\vec{E}} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \boxed{V = I R \quad \text{where } R = \rho\frac{L}{A} = \left(\frac{m}{n e^2 \tau}\right)\frac{L}{A}}$$

Where Resistivity $\rho = \frac{m}{n e^2 \tau}$ ($\Omega\cdot\text{m}$) and Conductivity $\sigma = \frac{1}{\rho} = n e \mu$ depend ONLY on the material and temperature—never on the length $L$ or area $A$ of the wire!

1.3 Wire Stretching ($R \propto L^2 \propto 1/r^4$) & Temperature Coefficient of Resistivity ($\alpha$)
  • Stretching or Recasting a Wire at Constant Volume ($V = A L = \text{Constant}$):
    When a wire is stretched so its length becomes $n L$, its cross-sectional area shrinks to $A/n$:
    $$\boxed{R = \rho\frac{L}{A} = \frac{\rho L^2}{V} = \frac{\rho V}{A^2} = \frac{\rho V}{\pi^2 r^4} \implies R \propto L^2 \propto \frac{1}{A^2} \propto \frac{1}{r^4}} \qquad \left(\text{For small }\% \text{ stretch: } \frac{\Delta R}{R} = 2\frac{\Delta L}{L} = -4\frac{\Delta r}{r}\right)$$
  • Temperature Dependence of Resistivity ($\rho_T = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$):
    • Metals / Conductors ($\alpha > 0$, Positive): As $T$ rises, collisions happen more frequently ($\tau$ decreases), so resistivity $\rho$ and resistance $R$ INCREASE with temperature.
    • Alloys (Nichrome, Manganin, Constantan): Very small positive $\alpha \approx 0$ and high $\rho$, used for standard resistance coils.
    • Semiconductors ($\text{Si, Ge}$) & Electrolytes ($\alpha < 0$, Negative): As $T$ rises, carrier density $n$ increases exponentially, so $\rho$ and $R$ DECREASE with temperature!
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of I = n e A v_d and Microscopic Resistivity ρ = m / (n e² τ)

Step 1: In time $dt$, all free electrons within distance $dx = v_d\,dt$ of a cross-section $A$ cross that plane. The volume swept is $dV = A v_d\,dt$, containing $dN = n(A v_d\,dt)$ electrons of total charge $dq = e\,dN = n e A v_d\,dt$. Dividing by $dt$ gives $\boxed{I = \frac{dq}{dt} = n e A v_d}$.

Step 2: Under electric field $E = \frac{V}{L}$, each electron experiences acceleration $a = \frac{eE}{m}$ for average relaxation time $\tau$ between collisions, acquiring drift speed $v_d = \frac{eE\tau}{m} = \frac{e\tau V}{m L}$. Substituting $v_d$ into $I = n e A v_d$:

$$I = n e A \left(\frac{e\tau V}{m L}\right) \implies \frac{V}{I} = R = \left(\frac{m}{n e^2 \tau}\right)\frac{L}{A} \implies \boxed{\rho = \frac{m}{n e^2 \tau}}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Current in a Non-Uniform Tapered Wire of Varying Cross-Section $A_1 > A_2$): In steady state, charge cannot pile up inside the wire, so Electric Current $I$ is 100% IDENTICAL at every cross-section ($I_1 = I_2$)! However, because $J = I/A$, $E = J/\sigma$, and $v_d = I/(neA)$ are all inversely proportional to area $A$, they are all LARGER at the narrower end ($J_2 > J_1, E_2 > E_1, v_{d2} > v_{d1}$)!
  • Trap 2 (Condition for Resistance of Two Series Wires to Be Independent of Temperature): For $R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2$ to remain constant at all temperatures, their temperature changes $\Delta R_1 + \Delta R_2 = 0$ must cancel: $\boxed{R_{10}\alpha_1 + R_{20}\alpha_2 = 0}$ (one must be a metal with $\alpha_1 > 0$ and the other a semiconductor/carbon with $\alpha_2 < 0$)!

topics.title: Resistor Networks, Cube Symmetry, Kirchhoff's Laws (KCL & KVL), Nodal Analysis & Grouping of Cells
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Series/Parallel Resistors, Cube Resistor Networks & Symmetry Rules
$$\text{Series (Same } I\text{):} \quad \boxed{R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2 + \dots} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Parallel (Same } V\text{):} \quad \boxed{\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \dots}$$

12 Identical Resistors (each of resistance $R$) Forming the Edges of a Cube (Memorize the 1-2-3 Shortcut: $\frac{7}{12}, \frac{3}{4}, \frac{5}{6}$!):

Terminals Connected Across CubeExact FractionEasy Memory Trick ($\frac{7}{12}, \frac{9}{12}, \frac{10}{12}$)
1. Across 1 Edge (Adjacent corners)$$\boxed{R_{\text{edge}} = \frac{7}{12}R}$$$\frac{7}{12}R$
2. Across Face Diagonal$$\boxed{R_{\text{face}} = \frac{3}{4}R}$$$\frac{9}{12}R = \frac{3}{4}R$
3. Across Body (Main) Diagonal (Opposite corners)$$\boxed{R_{\text{body}} = \frac{5}{6}R}$$$\frac{10}{12}R = \frac{5}{6}R$ (Derived from $\frac{R}{3} + \frac{R}{6} + \frac{R}{3}$)
2.2 Kirchhoff's Laws (KCL & KVL) & Zero-potential Nodal Method
  • 1. Kirchhoff's First Law (Junction Rule / KCL): At any junction, $\boxed{\sum I_{\text{entering}} = \sum I_{\text{leaving}}}$. Based on Conservation of Electric Charge.
  • 2. Kirchhoff's Second Law (Loop Rule / KVL): Around any closed loop, $\boxed{\sum \Delta V = 0}$. Based on Conservation of Energy (electrostatic field is conservative).
    • Moving across a resistor in the direction of current $I$: potential drops by $\mathbf{-IR}$.
    • Moving across a resistor against current $I$: potential rises by $\mathbf{+IR}$.
    • Moving across a battery from $-$ to $+$ terminal: $\mathbf{+\mathcal{E}}$; from $+$ to $-$ terminal: $\mathbf{-\mathcal{E}}$.
2.3 EMF ($\mathcal{E}$), Internal Resistance ($r$) & Series vs. Parallel Grouping of Cells
State of Cell (EMF $\mathcal{E}$, internal resistance $r$)Terminal Potential Difference ($V$)
1. Discharging (Current $I$ leaves $+$ terminal)$$\boxed{V = \mathcal{E} - I r} \quad (V < \mathcal{E})$$
2. Charging (External source pushes current $I$ INTO $+$ terminal)$$\boxed{V = \mathcal{E} + I r} \quad (V > \mathcal{E}!)$$
3. Open Circuit ($I = 0$) or Ideal Cell ($r = 0$)$$V = \mathcal{E}$$
4. Short Circuit ($R_{\text{ext}} = 0 \implies V = 0$)Maximum current $I_{\max} = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{r}$
$$\textbf{1. Series Cells:} \quad \boxed{\mathcal{E}_{\text{eq}} = \mathcal{E}_1 \pm \mathcal{E}_2 + \dots, \quad r_{\text{eq}} = r_1 + r_2 + \dots}$$
$$\textbf{2. Parallel Cells (Millman's Theorem — Very High Yield!):} \qquad \boxed{\mathcal{E}_{\text{eq}} = \frac{\frac{\mathcal{E}_1}{r_1} + \frac{\mathcal{E}_2}{r_2} + \dots}{\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2} + \dots} = \frac{\mathcal{E}_1 r_2 + \mathcal{E}_2 r_1}{r_1 + r_2}}, \qquad \boxed{\frac{1}{r_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2} + \dots}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Parallel Cell Equivalent EMF: E_eq = (E₁/r₁ + E₂/r₂) / (1/r₁ + 1/r₂)

Let two cells $(\mathcal{E}_1, r_1)$ and $(\mathcal{E}_2, r_2)$ be connected in parallel between nodes $A$ (potential $V$) and $B$ (potential $0$). The currents delivered by the two branches are $I_1 = \frac{\mathcal{E}_1 - V}{r_1}$ and $I_2 = \frac{\mathcal{E}_2 - V}{r_2}$. Total current is $I = I_1 + I_2$:

$$I = \left(\frac{\mathcal{E}_1}{r_1} + \frac{\mathcal{E}_2}{r_2}\right) - V\left(\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}\right) \implies V = \underbrace{\left(\frac{\frac{\mathcal{E}_1}{r_1} + \frac{\mathcal{E}_2}{r_2}}{\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}}\right)}_{\mathcal{E}_{\text{eq}}} - I \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}}\right)}_{r_{\text{eq}}}$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (One Cell Incorrectly Reversed in a Series Battery of $N$ Identical Cells): If $1$ cell out of $N$ identical cells in series is connected with reversed polarity, it cancels not only itself but also ONE other forward cell! Therefore, net EMF becomes $\boxed{\mathcal{E}_{\text{eq}} = (N - 2)\mathcal{E}}$ (NOT $(N-1)\mathcal{E}$!), while internal resistance STILL adds up for all $N$ cells: $\boxed{r_{\text{eq}} = N r}$!

topics.title: Joule Heating, Electric Bulbs (Series vs. Parallel), Maximum Power Transfer Theorem & Measuring Instruments (Bridge, Potentiometer, Galvanometer)
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Joule Heating, Rated Bulbs/Heaters & Maximum Power Transfer Theorem
$$\text{Electrical Power:} \quad \boxed{P = V I = I^2 R = \frac{V^2}{R}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Resistance of Appliance Rated } (P_R, V_R): \quad \boxed{R = \frac{V_R^2}{P_R} \implies R \propto \frac{1}{P_R}}$$

Crucial Insight: A $25\text{ W}, 220\text{ V}$ bulb has $4\times$ HIGHER resistance than a $100\text{ W}, 220\text{ V}$ bulb!

Appliance Connection ($R_1, R_2$ across supply $V$)Effective Power Consumed ($P_{\text{eq}}$)Brightness & Boiling Time Rules
1. Parallel Connection (Standard Home Wiring, same $V$)$$\boxed{P_{\text{eq}} = P_1 + P_2}$$
(Boiling time: $\frac{1}{t_p} = \frac{1}{t_1} + \frac{1}{t_2} \implies t_p = \frac{t_1 t_2}{t_1 + t_2}$)		$P = \frac{V^2}{R} \implies$ Higher rated wattage ($100\text{ W}$, smaller $R$) glows brighter!
2. Series Connection (Same current $I$)$$\boxed{\frac{1}{P_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{P_1} + \frac{1}{P_2} \implies P_{\text{eq}} = \frac{P_1 P_2}{P_1 + P_2}}$$
(Boiling time: $t_s = t_1 + t_2$)		$P = I^2 R \implies$ Lower rated wattage ($25\text{ W}$, larger $R$) glows brighter and fuses first if voltage is raised!
$$\textbf{Maximum Power Transfer Theorem:} \quad P_{\text{load}} = \left(\frac{\mathcal{E}}{R + r}\right)^2 R \text{ is MAXIMUM when } \boxed{R = r_{\text{internal}}} \implies \boxed{P_{\max} = \frac{\mathcal{E}^2}{4r}} \quad (\text{Efficiency } \eta = 50\%)$$
3.2 Electrical Measuring Instruments: Galvanometer Conversion, Bridges & Potentiometer
InstrumentCircuit Configuration & FormulaIdeal Resistance
1. Galvanometer ($G, I_g$) $\to$ Ammeter (Range $I$)Connect a small Shunt $S$ in PARALLEL with $G$:
$$\boxed{S = \frac{I_g G}{I - I_g}} \qquad \left(R_A = \frac{G S}{G + S}\right)$$		$R_{\text{ideal ammeter}} = 0$
2. Galvanometer ($G, I_g$) $\to$ Voltmeter (Range $V$)Connect a high Resistance $R_s$ in SERIES with $G$:
$$\boxed{R_s = \frac{V}{I_g} - G} \qquad (R_V = G + R_s)$$		$R_{\text{ideal voltmeter}} = \infty$
3. Balanced Wheatstone & Meter Bridge
(Zero current through central galvanometer, $V_B = V_D$)		$$\boxed{\frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Meter Bridge ($100\text{ cm}$ wire): } \boxed{\frac{R}{S} = \frac{\ell}{100 - \ell}}$$Independent of $R_G$ and battery EMF!
4. Potentiometer (Null-deflection ideal voltmeter, Potential Gradient $k = \frac{V_{AB}}{L}$)• Compare two EMFs: $\boxed{\frac{\mathcal{E}_1}{\mathcal{E}_2} = \frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}}$
• Internal resistance of cell: $\boxed{r = R\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2} - 1\right)}$		Draws ZERO current at balance ($R_{\text{eff}} = \infty$)!
topics.derivationHtml:
Calculus Proof of Maximum Power Transfer Theorem (R = r)

Power delivered by a cell $(\mathcal{E}, r)$ to an external load resistor $R$ is $P(R) = I^2 R = \frac{\mathcal{E}^2 R}{(R + r)^2}$. Differentiating with respect to $R$ and setting $\frac{dP}{dR} = 0$:

$$\frac{d}{dR}\left[\frac{R}{(R + r)^2}\right] = \frac{(R + r)^2(1) - R \cdot 2(R + r)}{(R + r)^4} = \frac{r - R}{(R + r)^3} = 0 \implies \boxed{R = r}$$

Or using algebra: $(R + r)^2 = (R - r)^2 + 4Rr$, so $P = \frac{\mathcal{E}^2 R}{(R - r)^2 + 4Rr} = \frac{\mathcal{E}^2}{\frac{(R - r)^2}{R} + 4r}$, which is clearly maximum when $(R - r)^2 = 0 \implies R = r$, giving $P_{\max} = \frac{\mathcal{E}^2}{4r}$!

R_eq = (P+Q)(R+S)/(P+Q+R+S)</text></g></svg>
topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Classic JEE Bulb Fusing Question): Suppose a $25\text{ W}, 220\text{ V}$ bulb and a $100\text{ W}, 220\text{ V}$ bulb are connected in series across a $440\text{ V}$ supply. Which bulb fuses? Since $R_{25} = 4 R_{100}$, in series the voltage divides in the ratio $4 : 1$! Thus the $25\text{ W}$ bulb gets $\frac{4}{5} \times 440\text{ V} = \mathbf{352\text{ V} > 220\text{ V}}$, so the $25\text{ W}$ bulb fuses immediately (while the $100\text{ W}$ bulb gets only $88\text{ V}$)!
  • Trap 2 (Interchanging the Battery and Galvanometer in a Balanced Wheatstone Bridge): If $\frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}$, then $\frac{P}{R} = \frac{Q}{S}$ is also automatically true! Therefore, interchanging the positions of the battery and the galvanometer does NOT disturb the null balance of a Wheatstone bridge!

topics.title: RC Circuits: Charging & Discharging of a Capacitor, Time Constant (τ = RC) & Initial vs. Steady-State Shortcuts
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 The Two-Instant Shortcut: How a Capacitor Behaves at $t = 0^+$ vs. $t \to \infty$
90% of JEE RC Circuit Questions Only Ask for $t = 0^+$ or $t \to \infty$:
  • At $t = 0^+$ (Just After Closing Switch, Uncharged Capacitor $q = 0$): Since $V_C = \frac{q}{C} = 0$, an uncharged capacitor acts like a CLOSED WIRE (SHORT CIRCUIT, Zero Resistance!).
  • At $t \to \infty$ (Steady State, Long Time After Closing Switch): The capacitor is fully charged ($I_C = 0$), so the capacitor branch acts like an OPEN CIRCUIT (BROKEN WIRE, Infinite Resistance!). Find the voltage $V_{\text{steady}}$ across the open terminals using simple resistor divider rules, and set $Q_{\max} = C V_{\text{steady}}$!
4.2 Exact Exponential Equations for Charging & Discharging an RC Circuit ($\tau = R_{\text{eq}} C$)
Quantity1. Charging from $q=0$ ($Q_0 = C\mathcal{E}$)2. Discharging from Initial Charge $Q_0$
Charge on Capacitor $q(t)$$$\boxed{q(t) = Q_0\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)}$$
(At $t = \tau = RC$: $q = 0.632\,Q_0$)		$$\boxed{q(t) = Q_0 e^{-t/\tau}}$$
(At $t = \tau = RC$: $q = 0.368\,Q_0$)
Voltage Across Capacitor $V_C(t)$$$V_C(t) = \mathcal{E}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)$$$$V_C(t) = V_0 e^{-t/\tau}$$
Current in Resistor $I(t)$$$\boxed{I(t) = \frac{dq}{dt} = \left(\frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}\right)e^{-t/\tau} = I_0 e^{-t/\tau}}$$$$\boxed{I(t) = -\frac{dq}{dt} = \left(\frac{Q_0}{RC}\right)e^{-t/\tau} = I_0 e^{-t/\tau}}$$

How to Find Time Constant $\tau = R_{\text{th}} C$ for Multi-Resistor Circuits:
1. Short-circuit all ideal voltage sources (replace batteries with plain wires).
2. Find the equivalent resistance $R_{\text{th}}$ of the resistor network as seen between the two terminals of the capacitor $C$.
3. Then $\boxed{\tau = R_{\text{th}} C}$!
topics.derivationHtml:
Differential Equation Derivation of Capacitor Charging q(t) = C E (1 − e⁻ᵗ/ᴿᶜ)

Apply Kirchhoff's Loop Rule around a series circuit of battery $\mathcal{E}$, resistor $R$, and capacitor $C$ ($I = \frac{dq}{dt}$):

$$\mathcal{E} - I R - \frac{q}{C} = 0 \implies R\frac{dq}{dt} = \frac{C\mathcal{E} - q}{C} \implies \int_0^q \frac{dq}{C\mathcal{E} - q} = \int_0^t \frac{dt}{RC}$$

Integrating both sides gives $-\ln\left(\frac{C\mathcal{E} - q}{C\mathcal{E}}\right) = \frac{t}{RC} \implies 1 - \frac{q}{C\mathcal{E}} = e^{-t/(RC)} \implies \boxed{q(t) = C\mathcal{E}\left(1 - e^{-t/(RC)}\right)}$.

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Current $I(t)$ Decays Exponentially During BOTH Charging AND Discharging!): Students often think current $I(t)$ grows like $(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$ during charging. NO! Charge $q(t)$ grows as $(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$, which means its derivative $I(t) = \frac{dq}{dt} = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}e^{-t/\tau}$ is maximum at $t = 0^+$ and decays to zero as $t \to \infty$ in both charging and discharging!

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 17: Current Electricity & RC Circuits! With drift velocity, Kirchhoff networks, electrical instruments, and RC transients complete, you are ready to enter Magnetism in Chapter 18.
summary:
• Microscopic Ohm's Law: $I = neAv_d$, $v_d = \frac{eE\tau}{m}$, $\rho = \frac{m}{ne^2\tau}$; Wire stretching $R \propto L^2 \propto 1/r^4$.
  • Cells & Power: Discharging $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$; Parallel cells $\mathcal{E}_{\text{eq}} = \frac{\mathcal{E}_1/r_1 + \mathcal{E}_2/r_2}{1/r_1 + 1/r_2}$; Max power at $R = r$ ($P_{\max} = \frac{\mathcal{E}^2}{4r}$).
  • Instruments: Ammeter shunt $S = \frac{I_g G}{I - I_g}$; Voltmeter series $R_s = \frac{V}{I_g} - G$; Meter bridge $\frac{R}{S} = \frac{\ell}{100-\ell}$; Potentiometer $r = R\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2} - 1\right)$.
  • RC Circuits: $\tau = R_{\text{th}}C$; $t = 0^+$ uncharged capacitor is a short circuit; $t \to \infty$ capacitor is an open circuit.

Parallel Cells (Millman)$\mathcal{E}_{\text{eq}} = \dfrac{\mathcal{E}_1 r_2 + \mathcal{E}_2 r_1}{r_1 + r_2}, \quad r_{\text{eq}} = \dfrac{r_1 r_2}{r_1 + r_2}$Flip sign of $\mathcal{E}_2$ if polarity is reversed.

Ammeter & Voltmeter$S = \dfrac{I_g G}{I - I_g} \text{ (parallel)}, \quad R_s = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G \text{ (series)}$Ideal Ammeter $R=0$; Ideal Voltmeter $R=\infty$.

questions.prompt: A cylindrical copper wire of resistance $R = 10\,\Omega$ is uniformly stretched through a die until its radius becomes half of its original radius ($r' = r/2$), keeping its volume constant. What is the new resistance of the wire?
questions.explanation: At constant volume, $R \propto \frac{1}{r^4}$. When radius is halved ($r' = r/2$), the resistance increases by $2^4 = 16$ times: $R' = 16 \times 10\,\Omega = 160\,\Omega$.

questions.prompt: Two cells of EMFs $\mathcal{E}_1 = 6\text{ V}$ (internal resistance $r_1 = 1\,\Omega$) and $\mathcal{E}_2 = 3\text{ V}$ (internal resistance $r_2 = 2\,\Omega$) are connected in parallel with their positive terminals joined together. What is the equivalent EMF $\mathcal{E}_{\text{eq}}$ of the combination?
Two electric bulbs, one rated $25\text{ W}, 220\text{ V}$ and the other rated $100\text{ W}, 220\text{ V}$, are connected in series across a $440\text{ V}$ mains supply. Which bulb will fuse?
questions.explanation: Since $R = V_R^2 / P_R$, the resistance ratio is $\frac{R_{25}}{R_{100}} = \frac{100}{25} = 4 : 1$. In series across $440\text{ V}$, voltage divides proportional to resistance, so the $25\text{ W}$ bulb gets $V_{25} = \frac{4}{4+1}(440\text{ V}) = 352\text{ V} > 220\text{ V}$, causing the $25\text{ W}$ bulb to fuse immediately!

questions.prompt: A moving-coil galvanometer of resistance $G = 99\,\Omega$ gives full-scale deflection for a current $I_g = 10\text{ mA}$. What shunt resistance $S$ must be connected in parallel with it to convert it into an ammeter of range $0$ to $1\text{ A}$?
In a meter bridge experiment, a resistance $R$ in the left gap and $S = 12\,\Omega$ in the right gap produce a null balance point at $\ell = 40\text{ cm}$ from the left end. What is the value of $R$?
questions.explanation: At balance in a meter bridge, $\frac{R}{S} = \frac{\ell}{100 - \ell} = \frac{40}{60} = \frac{2}{3} \implies R = \frac{2}{3}(12\,\Omega) = 8\,\Omega$.

questions.prompt: In a potentiometer experiment, a cell of EMF $\mathcal{E}$ balances at a length $\ell_1 = 240\text{ cm}$. When a resistor $R = 4\,\Omega$ is shunted across the cell, the balancing length drops to $\ell_2 = 160\text{ cm}$. What is the internal resistance $r$ of the cell?

Twelve identical wires, each of resistance $R = 6\,\Omega$, are joined to form the 12 edges of a skeleton cube. A current enters at one corner and leaves at the diagonally opposite body corner. What is the equivalent resistance between these two corners?
questions.explanation: Across the body diagonal of a cube of 12 identical resistors $R$, the equivalent resistance is $R_{\text{body}} = \frac{5}{6}R = \frac{5}{6}(6\,\Omega) = 5\,\Omega$.

questions.prompt: An uncharged capacitor of capacitance $C = 5\,\mu\text{F}$ is connected in series with a resistor $R = 200\,\text{k}\Omega$ and a battery of $\mathcal{E} = 20\text{ V}$. At what time $t$ after closing the switch does the potential difference across the resistor equal the potential difference across the capacitor ($V_R = V_C$)? (Take $\ln 2 = 0.693$)
questions.explanation: Time constant $\tau = RC = (2 \times 10^5\,\Omega)(5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}) = 1.0\text{ s}$. Since $V_R + V_C = \mathcal{E}$, $V_R = V_C$ occurs when $V_C = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{2} \implies \mathcal{E}(1 - e^{-t/\tau}) = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{2} \implies e^{-t/\tau} = \frac{1}{2} \implies t = \tau\ln 2 = 1.0 \times 0.693 = 0.693\text{ s}$.
